forces.title: Structural import dependence heightens geopolitical vulnerability
forces.description: India's fertiliser value chain, especially for Urea and Di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), has significant import dependence, which increased materially to ~34% in FY26 from ~23% in FY25. This structural reliance on imports, particularly from West Asia for urea (37% of imports) and Gulf countries for natural gas (85% of fertiliser sector's gas requirement), makes the sector highly vulnerable to supply disruptions and shipping delays caused by geopolitical conflicts like the West Asia crisis.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: Rising global energy and raw material prices due to West Asia conflict
forces.description: The ongoing West Asia crisis has sharply increased international prices of Urea and DAP, as well as key raw materials like ammonia (~60% increase), sulphur (~50% increase), and natural gas (spot prices from ~$10/mmbtu to >$15/mmbtu). This surge directly intensifies cost pressures across the fertiliser sector, compressing profit margins, especially for NPK players, and making imports economically unviable for DAP due to fixed retail prices.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: FY27 fertiliser subsidy budget likely to fall short
forces.description: The government has budgeted Rs 1.71 lakh crore for fertiliser subsidy in FY27. However, the recent surge in import prices of gas, key raw materials, and finished fertilisers suggests that these budgeted allocations will again fall short of actual requirements, necessitating significant supplementary grants. This shortfall creates uncertainty for manufacturers, potentially impacting their profitability and cash flows if the government faces financial strain or delays payments, as fiscal deficit often constrains subsidy budgets.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: Below-normal monsoon threatens agricultural production and demand
forces.description: The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast a sub-normal monsoon for CY2026 at 92% of the long-period average (LPA) due to El Niño. This raises concerns about agricultural production, especially kharif sowing (down 16% as of July 10th), which in turn could lead to region-specific demand variability and affect overall fertiliser consumption, thereby acting as a headwind for the sector's growth and profitability. The temporal and spatial distribution of rainfall in July and August will be critical.

forces.title: Increased domestic production supporting self-reliance
forces.description: India has been proactively enhancing its domestic fertiliser production capacity, with urea production reaching its highest-ever of 314 lakh metric tonnes (LMT) in 2023-24, and 306.67 LMT in 2024-25. Total domestic fertiliser production was around 503 LMT in 2023-24 against a consumption of 601 LMT. This increasing domestic output reduces India's reliance on imports, enhancing fertiliser security and buffering against global supply disruptions and price volatility, even as near-term import dependency has seen a reversal.

forces.title: Government subsidy allocation crucial for sector profitability
forces.description: The government's allocation of Rs 1.71 lakh crore for fertiliser subsidy in FY27, including urea and NBS, is a primary policy revenue variable that directly improves the profitability and financial health of manufacturers. This compensates for the gap between production costs and controlled farmer prices. Timely subsidy releases in recent years have reduced receivable build-up and supported working capital management, allowing the sector to better absorb input price volatility.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: Biogas/CBG as alternative domestic feedstock for fertilisers
forces.description: Biogas and compressed biogas (CBG) offer a strategic domestic alternative to partially substitute natural gas in fertiliser production. Upgraded biogas can serve as a renewable feedstock for hydrogen production, crucial for ammonia synthesis, reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels. Additionally, biogas produces digestate, which can be processed into organic fertilisers like phosphate-rich organic manure (PROM), simultaneously reducing dependence on synthetic fertilisers and improving soil quality. The GOBARDHAN initiative provides a framework for scaling such systems.
forces.source_title: From LNG dependence to domestic resilience: Securing India's fertiliser future

forces.title: Increased MSPs and acreage boost fertiliser demand
forces.description: Fertiliser demand for the upcoming Kharif season is expected to be supported by a continued increase in Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for major crops and improving acreage. Higher MSPs enhance farmer profitability and income stability, directly boosting their purchasing power and demand for fertilisers. Simultaneously, increased cultivated area necessitates greater use of fertilisers to support crop growth and yields, providing a stable demand base for the industry.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: Comfortable fertiliser inventory levels provide short-term cushion
forces.description: Amidst ongoing geopolitical uncertainty, the Government of India has ensured that overall fertiliser stocks remain relatively comfortable, standing at around 40% of the Kharif season requirement as of March 31, 2026, and improving to 49% by April 2026 (versus a normal level of 33%). This better inventory position helps soften the immediate risk of a supply squeeze and provides a near-term cushion ahead of the Kharif sowing season, mitigating short-term supply chain disruptions.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: Lower domestic gas allocations affect urea capacity utilization
forces.description: Capacity utilisation in the fertiliser sector, particularly for urea production, has been negatively affected in recent months by lower domestic gas allocations. As natural gas is the majority feedstock for urea, reduced availability directly impacts production volumes and operational efficiency for manufacturers. This forces greater reliance on higher-priced imported gas or reduces overall output, contributing to increased import dependence and cost pressures across the sector.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: Fiscal deficit threatens fertiliser subsidies and financing costs
forces.description: A rising fiscal deficit (both absolute and as a percentage of GDP) signals government financial strain. For the fertiliser sector, this carries the risk of pressure to reduce fertiliser subsidies or delay payments, negatively impacting profitability and cash flows. Additionally, increased government borrowing can lead to higher interest rates, which would raise financing costs for capital-intensive fertiliser projects and for working capital requirements due to import financing and potential subsidy payment delays, thereby increasing borrowings by the sector.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

forces.title: Government support for agriculture sector boosts demand
forces.description: Higher government expenditure on the agriculture sector generally boosts farmer incomes and overall agricultural activity. This directly translates to increased demand for inputs like fertilisers, as farmers have greater capacity and incentive to invest in improving crop yields. Such policy support enhances the fundamental demand drivers for the fertiliser industry, creating a positive environment for sales volumes and market stability.
forces.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

viewpoints.title: FY27 fertiliser sector faces challenges despite stronger credit profile
viewpoints.description: CareEdge Ratings views the FY27 outlook for the fertiliser sector as challenging due to the West Asia geopolitical crisis driving up natural gas and raw material prices. Despite this, the sector is better positioned to absorb volatility thanks to timely subsidy releases in recent years. However, rising import dependence, cost escalations, and a below-normal monsoon forecast for CY26 will keep the sector on edge and likely increase subsidy requirements, potentially leading to higher borrowings for working capital.
viewpoints.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

viewpoints.title: India's fertiliser security needs strategic shift beyond short-term measures
viewpoints.description: KPMG states that India's fertiliser security is intrinsically linked to its energy strategy, with structural dependence on imported LNG and natural gas transmitting global energy market disruptions directly into domestic agriculture. Current responses of subsidies and reallocations only stabilize outcomes without reducing underlying dependency. A strategic shift is required to reduce systemic exposure to volatility by diversifying feedstock sources, integrating biogas, and supporting renewable hydrogen, moving towards a resilient and domestically anchored fertiliser energy model.
viewpoints.source_title: From LNG dependence to domestic resilience: Securing India's fertiliser future

demand_drivers.description: Natural gas is a critical hydrocarbon feedstock chemically converted to extract hydrogen for ammonia synthesis, which underpins urea and other nitrogen-based fertilisers.
CGD sector is a major consumer of Regasified Liquefied Natural Gas (RLNG) alongside fertilisers.

market_sizing.methodology: India’s total natural gas consumption in 2023-24 was around 188 MMSCMD, with domestic production at 98 MMSCMD and LNG imports at 90 MMSCMD. Fertilisers and City Gas Distribution (CGD) sectors account for the highest Regasified Liquefied Natural Gas (RLNG) consumption.
market_sizing.source_title: From LNG dependence to domestic resilience: Securing India's fertiliser future

pnl_drivers.description: The allocated subsidy directly improves the profitability and financial health of fertiliser manufacturers by covering the gap between production costs and controlled farmer prices.

market_sizing.methodology: The Government of India budgeted Rs 1.71 lakh crore for fertiliser subsidy in FY27. This comprises Rs 1.17 lakh crore for urea subsidy and Rs 0.54 lakh crore for Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS).
market_sizing.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget

demand_drivers.description: Fertiliser consumption is estimated to have grown by ~3% in FY26, requiring additional supply.
Domestic production marginally declined to ~517 LMT from ~518 LMT in FY25, creating a supply gap.
Increased imports were also aimed at building buffer stock for the upcoming kharif season to counter geopolitical uncertainty.

market_sizing.methodology: India's fertiliser imports are estimated to have risen sharply to ~249 LMT in FY26 from ~160 LMT in FY25, meeting the gap between consumption (~3% growth) and marginally declined domestic production (~517 LMT). This increase was to ensure adequate stocks for the upcoming kharif season amidst geopolitical uncertainty.
market_sizing.source_title: Fertiliser Sector Impact of West Asia Crisis on Availability & Subsidy Budget
